**Ambitious Science Teaching**, Mark Windschitl, Jessica Thompson, and Melissa Braaten (Harvard Education Press, 2018; ISBN 9781682531624) — a book of advice about how to teach science, organized around four sets of core practices. Not a standard; nothing in it is tested.
Publisher: https://hep.gse.harvard.edu/9781682531624/ambitious-science-teaching/ · ERIC record: https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED583076

**ambitiousscienceteaching.org** — the free companion site with the practice sets, primers, tools, and video.
https://ambitiousscienceteaching.org/
> "Ambitious teaching can be learned. Ambitious Science Teaching supports students in tackling authentic and meaningful science phenomena with attention to students' histories, social interactions, and local and global communities."
The four practice sets: planning for engagement with important science ideas; eliciting students' ideas; supporting ongoing changes in thinking; pressing for evidence-based explanations.

**C2AST: Critical and Cultural Approaches to Ambitious Science Teaching** — Thompson, Mawyer, Johnson, Scipio, and Luehmann, *The Science Teacher*, September/October 2021 — the critical and cultural extension of AST; again advice, not a standard.
https://www.nsta.org/science-teacher/science-teacher-septemberoctober-2021/c2ast-critical-and-cultural-approaches

**(a) Massachusetts calls its standards documents "curriculum frameworks."** The naming is exactly the confusion: the document is standards, not curriculum, and it says so inside.
DESE frameworks page: https://www.doe.mass.edu/frameworks/ · current list: https://www.doe.mass.edu/frameworks/current.html
> "The Massachusetts Curriculum Frameworks provide teachers, students and families with clear and shared expectations for what all students should know and be able to do at the end of each year." (DESE)
*2016 Massachusetts Science and Technology/Engineering Curriculum Framework* (https://www.doe.mass.edu/frameworks/scitech/2016-04.pdf), under the heading "Relationship of Standards to Curriculum and Instruction":
> "The standards are outcomes, or goals, that reflect what a student should know and be able to do. They do not dictate a manner or methods of teaching. The standards are written in a way that expresses the concept and skills to be achieved and demonstrated by students, but leaves curricular and instructional decisions to districts, schools, and teachers. The standards are not a set of instructional activities or assessment tasks."

**(b) Rigid pacing versus teacher judgment.** Jane L. David, "What Research Says About… Pacing Guides," *Educational Leadership*, October 1, 2008, Vol. 66, No. 2 (ASCD).
https://www.ascd.org/el/articles/pacing-guides
> "Teachers are caught between a rock and a hard place: Slow down and risk lack of coverage, or speed up and sacrifice depth of learning."
> "Cobb, McClain, de Silva Lamberg, and Dean (2003) found that in the United States, most guides do not address the development of student reasoning and that teachers rarely deviate from the guides."
The same article notes the other side — new teachers "can benefit from resources such as pacing guides designed to help them figure out what to teach and how."

## From the standards to Tuesday's lesson

A standard says what most children should be able to do by the end of a grade. A lesson plan narrows that down to one piece of one day. Here is how that narrowing works for Ms. Boyd's Lesson 1, and where her plan's own codes went wrong.

| Source | What it says | How it narrows to Lesson 1 |
|---|---|---|
| **Her unit plan** | 4.PS1.1 and 4.PS1.2, copied from a 2009 kit's alignment sheet | **Neither code exists in Tennessee's current standards.** There is no grade-4 matter strand. |
| **Tennessee, grade 3** | 3.PS1.1: "Develop a model of solids, liquids, and gasses to describe that each state of matter is made of particles too small to be seen." | Room 14 met this last year. "Name the three states of matter" reviews it. |
| **Tennessee, grade 4** | 4.ESS2.1: "Collect and analyze data from observations to provide evidence that rocks, soils, and sediments are broken into smaller pieces through mechanical weathering (e.g., frost wedging, abrasion, tree root wedging) and are transported by water, ice, wind, gravity, and vegetation." | The class studied frost wedging in November. Water expanding as it freezes, which is what split the rocks, is also what split Aaliyah's pipe. |
| **Tennessee, grade 5** | 5.PS1.1: "Analyze and interpret data from observations and measurements of the physical properties of matter to explain phase changes between a solid, liquid, or gas." | Where the unit is headed: explaining a change of state with evidence. Lesson 3 ("water is strange") is the step toward it. |
| **NGSS** | 2-PS1-4 (heating and cooling changes, some reversible); 5-PS1-1 (matter is made of particles too small to be seen); 4-ESS2-1 (evidence of weathering by water, ice, wind, or vegetation). Full text below. | The national performance expectations bracket the same idea from second grade to fifth. Tennessee did not adopt NGSS; it wrote its own standards from the same national framework. |
| **The framework (AST)** | Practice Set 1: choose a phenomenon that needs the target ideas to explain it; launch it; draw out what students already think. | Lesson 1's job is the launch: a puzzling event, and the children's first ideas about it. Not the explanation. |
| **Lesson 1's objective, as she wrote it** | "I can notice and wonder about a frozen lake. I can name the three states of matter." | Noticing and wondering serves the launch. Naming the states reviews grade 3. Neither asks yet for the grade-4 and grade-5 idea; her plan saves that for Lesson 3. |

**What to take from this.** Her plan's codes are decoration, but her *unit* is coherent: it reviews grade 3, reaches back to the grade-4 weathering unit, and builds toward grade 5. When you plan your own launch at the end of this unit, you'll choose which of these standards it serves.

You are Dr. Adaeze Okafor, methods instructor, reading a teacher candidate's Launch Study back to them. Your rules, which you never break: you quote the candidate's own words before you say anything about them; you never praise before you have read; you say "No" and then explain when you disagree; you never use "belonging" or "ways of knowing" without naming the specific child and the specific move; you never tell the candidate what they think; you never end with a summary of what they have learned or a pep talk about next time. Short sentences. One question at a time. No exclamation marks. Dry; your warmth arrives late and briefly.

The session: the candidate read the transcript of Ms. Boyd launching her fourth-grade unit, Investigating Matter, with a frozen Michigan lake, with her unit plan and lesson plan in hand. Facts the candidate could find: the unit's standard codes are copied from a 2009 kit and do not exist in Tennessee, which the session treats as decoration, since a standard is a growth chart and not a menu; the unit itself reviews Tennessee 3.PS1.1, reaches back to 4.ESS2.1 (frost wedging) and builds toward 5.PS1.1; Aaliyah's burst pipe at minute six was Lesson 3 of the unit and the same physics as the weathering unit the class did in November; Bri's question was on the anticipated list and got charted, Aaliyah's was not and got "later"; the plan said do not cold-call Diego and she did. Four peers argued with the candidate: Jordan, who defends Ms. Boyd on classroom management; Nyota, who rejects the premise that a phenomenon must come from children's lives; Dwayne, who asks the plain question; and Luke, a conservative who argues for explicit instruction and a knowledge-rich curriculum, distrusts the equity framing, and agrees that Diego was failed. The candidate then replayed the launch making Ms. Boyd's moves against the clock, and planned their own launch of the same science for the same room.

What the candidate wrote (quote from these; do not invent):
Discourse read:
Replay path, as Ms. Boyd, from minute 10 (a blank means that fork never arose on their path): Marcus:

.
Their account of their participation choices, what those choices made possible and what they cost:
. Knowledge from home, and a painful disclosure:

Write five to eight sentences of Markdown, first person, as yourself. In order: quote one strong move of theirs, from the plan or the replay, and say why it is strong in terms of a named child. Then press on one thing, the most useful of: whether their plan keeps guidance and knowledge-building visible rather than hoping they emerge from the phenomenon (the evidence on unguided exploration is against hoping); whether their off-path plan can tell Jaylen's candy from Keisha's salt; whether Diego has a way in that is a thing he does, not a sentence about him; or whether their account of their participation choices names what those choices cost. Tie the press to their words. If the candidate rejected the premise of the session anywhere, restate their argument fairly in one sentence, say what in the transcript supports it and what cuts against it, and do not pretend they agreed; a well-argued dissent is a strong study. ## The phenomenon: how Ms. Boyd introduces it

*Room 14, fourth grade, Tuesday at 1:15: the first day of her unit, Investigating Matter. You were at the back of the room. These are the first four minutes, word for word.*

**[Ms. Boyd dims the lights and plays a short clip: a wide, snow-rimmed lake, small figures skating in the distance.]**

**Ms. Boyd:** This is Torch Lake, up in Michigan, where I grew up. Every winter the whole top froze so solid we'd skate on it, and my dad would drill a hole and go ice fishing. Here's what puzzled me as a kid: if the lake freezes over, how are the fish down underneath still alive and swimming? Turn and tell your partner what you think.

*[Students talk in pairs. Ms. Boyd circulates, then calls them back.]*

**Ms. Boyd:** Okay — who can tell me what they think is happening?

**Marcus:** My grandpa takes me ice fishing when we visit my cousins up north! The fish are fine because the ice is only on the top.

**Ms. Boyd:** Exactly, Marcus — the ice is only on top. Great. So why *only* on top?

**Aaliyah:** In the big freeze last year our pipes busted and water went all in the hallway. My mama said the ice broke the pipe.

**Ms. Boyd:** Ooh — we'll get to ice and pipes later. Right now let's stay with our lake. So, why does the ice float on top instead of sinking to the bottom?

**Bri:** Wait — if ice is just frozen water, why doesn't it sink? It's the same stuff.

**Ms. Boyd:** Good question, Bri — hold onto it. Here's an easier one first. Who can name the three states of matter for me?

**Darnell:** Solid, liquid, and gas!

**Ms. Boyd:** Yes! Solid, liquid, gas. *[She writes them on the board.]* And ice — is that a solid, a liquid, or a gas?

**Class:** Solid!

**Ms. Boyd:** Right. Now — what do you think would happen to a bottle of water if I left it in the freezer overnight; would it stay the same? … It would freeze into ice, of course. So, back to Bri's question: ice is lighter than water, which is why it floats and the fish are safe down below. We're going to spend the whole unit on the states of matter. Diego, can you read the three states off the board for us? … Diego? … Okay — Marcus, read them for us.

*[Diego looks down and doesn't answer.]*
